Kozmik Yolculuğun En Kritik Adımı İçin Buradayız.

Biz, geleceğin uzay misyonları için en güvenli, en akıllı ve en stratejik iniş noktalarını tasarlayan bir NASA Space Apps takımıyız. Verileri keşfe, keşifleri güvenli birer adıma dönüştürerek insanlığın yıldızlar arasındaki izini sürüyor; bilinmeyene atılacak o ilk adımı sağlam temeller üzerine kuruyoruz. Çünkü gökyüzüne ulaşmak sadece bir başlangıçtır; asıl mesele, oraya güvenle inebilmektir.
summary:
Moon Navigator is a project by team CHARMAQ, developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It starts from a simple problem: at the Moon’s south pole, a landing can be lost to a single shadow chosen at the wrong hour.

The challenge we chose asks for a website that compares the landings made at the lunar south pole, and their dates, in a way that is easy to understand. Our goal is to turn complex lunar data into an experience people can explore. Planners can run calculations for future landings, observers can review landings that have already taken place, and enthusiasts can learn about south pole landings.

The website works in five steps:

Select a region: the user picks a region on the simulated Moon.
Date and time: a past or future moment is set.
Ambient light: the site determines the sunlight suitable for flight.
Landing simulation: past flights are replayed under the same conditions.
Result: the site shows whether conditions are suitable and gives a success rate, with reasons.

Beyond the simulator, the site includes a weekly safety ranking, a comparison tool, a sky calendar with asteroid tracking, a mission guide, a knowledge base and references.

The team has six members: Mehmet Mirza Önal (coordinator, captain, developer), İkra Nuray Çevik (researcher, data analysis), Hatice Kübra Şahan (data analysis), Serra Kaya (researcher), Metehan Karayılan (developer) and Taner Efe Karabaş (developer). The project draws on NASA’s Moon Missions page and NASA Moon Trek.
details:
Moon Navigator is a web-based project developed by team CHARMAQ for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It addresses the challenge of comparing landings at the Moon’s south pole, together with their dates, in a way that is clear and easy to understand. The project takes complex lunar data and turns it into an interactive experience that anyone can explore.

The problem

Landing at the lunar south pole depends heavily on timing and lighting. A site that is suitable at one moment may be in shadow at another, so a landing can fail because of a single shadow chosen at the wrong hour. The data needed to judge this is complex and hard for non-experts to read.

Project goal

We designed a website that makes this data explorable. It lets users run calculations and learn about landings at the south pole, covering both landings that have already taken place and landings that could be carried out in the future.

Who it is for

  • Planners, who want to run calculations for possible future landings.
  • Observers, who want to review landings that have already happened.
  • Enthusiasts, who want to learn about south pole landings.

How the website works

  1. Select a region. The user chooses a region on the simulated Moon.
  2. Change the date and time. The user sets a moment in the past or in the future.
  3. Ambient light. The site determines the sunlight conditions suitable for flight at that place and time.
  4. Simulate the landing. The site simulates the landing and can replay past flights under the same conditions, time and parameters.
  5. See the result. The site shows whether conditions are suitable for the selected landing. If a landing is made, it gives the success rate together with the reasons behind it.

Additional sections of the site

  • Weekly safety ranking
  • Comparison
  • Sky calendar and asteroid tracking
  • Mission guide
  • Knowledge base
  • References
